newsitem.title: USA: New 'hired-gun' consultants shake up U.S. politics.
newsitem.headline: New 'hired-gun' consultants shake up U.S. politics.

text.p: A new breed of political consultant -- brash, limelight-loving and tied to no party -- is making some in Washington's old guard long for the days when campaigns were run by an anonymous circle of loyalists.

There was a time when the general public never knew the faces, let alone the names, of strategists in a presidential campaign. Now it would be hard for them not to know, among others, Dick Morris, who until a much-chronicled fall from grace was a top campaign adviser to President Bill Clinton.

"In a sense they're all hired guns, though very few of them have the opportunities of a Dick Morris to cross party lines," said Stephen Hess, who has advised both Republican and Democratic presidents.

"They do all share something in common and that is that they have an independent persona that is beyond the people that they work for," said Hess, who now works at the Brookings Institute. "They always have their eye on the main chance."
Morris exemplifies the genre -- a self-styled liberal in his youth, he has worked for Democrats and Republicans, occasionally in the same congressional district.

When a supermarket tabloid reported, and Morris did not deny, a long-term liaison with a $200-an-hour prostitute, he left Clinton's campaign but held the spotlight, holding a televised news conference at his home and appearing on the cover of a newsmagazine with his wife.
Morris is by no means the only publicity-seeking "switch-hitter" in American political consulting.

Ed Rollins, a long-time Republican strategist who once crowed about suppressing the black vote in the New Jersey governor's race that put Christine Todd Whitman in the statehouse, apparently had no qualms about working for independent presidential candidate Ross Perot in 1992.
David Gergen, who worked for Republican presidents Richard Nixon, Gerald Ford and Ronald Reagan, was brought into the Democratic Clinton administration as counsellor to the president in 1993.

Also on the Republican side, volunteer consultant Roger Stone seeped into the public consciousness last week when a photograph of his scantily clad wife, a former model, appeared in newspapers along with an account of sexual advertisements placed in the couple's name on the Internet.

Far from hiding from the publicity, Stone, who had worked for Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole's campaign, appeared on a television news programme, Fox News Sunday, to deny that he or his wife had placed the ads and defend his right to a private life.

Even consultants who stay with one party -- for example, Clinton adviser James Carville, who became a morning talk show staple in the 1992 campaign season -- are far more famous than the anonymous, in-house teams of advisers who used to guide presidential candidates.

Television may have helped create the need for the modern-style consultant to help a candidate dress, talk and move in a telegenic way. But Hess believes technical aspects of campaigning in the 1990s, including sophisticated polling and advertising purchases, require experts in these fields.

Where do the experts come from? There are now college courses in political consulting, contrasting with the path earlier consultants usually took: years of work for a party or a candidate to gain experience.

This proliferation of consultants troubles Washington insider Meg Greenfield, editorial page editor of the Washington Post. "(T)here is a horrid logic to the Morris story: the absence finally of loyalty to the candidate and the absence of respect for the confidences of the campaign," Greenfield wrote in Newsweek magazine.
